explanations.name: Rating
explanations.text: The rating is a mean-reversion trigger score from the 3 voting indicators (Bollinger, Stochastic, RSI): +1/-1 = Lean Buy/Lean Sell, +2/-2 = Buy/Sell, +3/-3 = Strong Buy/Strong Sell, 0 = Hold. Trend (50/200 EMA) is shown next to the rating as context but does NOT vote — otherwise a dip to oversold would always be cancelled out by the downtrend votes and everything would read Hold.

explanations.name: 50 EMA
explanations.text: Medium-term trend context (~10 weeks) — shown, not counted in the score. Price above = uptrend. Price below = downtrend. Reacts faster than the 200 EMA — useful for catching trend changes earlier.

explanations.name: 200 EMA
explanations.text: Long-term trend context (~40 weeks) — shown, not counted in the score. The institutional bull/bear benchmark. When the 50 EMA is above the 200 EMA the rating shows 'golden cross' (bullish regime); below shows 'death cross'. A downtrend raises the bar for buying a dip (falling-knife risk).

explanations.name: Bollinger Bands
explanations.text: Measures price relative to a 20-day volatility range (±2 std deviations). Near lower band = oversold, price cheap vs recent range. Mid-range = neutral. Near upper band = overbought, price stretched. Mean reversion signal — extreme readings suggest a move back toward the middle.

explanations.name: RSI
explanations.text: Momentum gauge — measures the speed of recent gains vs losses. Votes on absolute levels: below 30 = oversold (buy vote), above 70 = overbought (sell vote), in between = neutral. Whether RSI is rising or falling vs its own 14-day average is shown in brackets as momentum context but doesn't vote.

explanations.name: Stochastic
explanations.text: Where today's close sits within the 14-day high-low range. Below 20 = oversold, price near recent lows. 20-80 = neutral. Above 80 = overbought, price near recent highs. In a strong downtrend, can stay below 20 for weeks — oversold doesn't always mean imminent bounce.

explanations.name: Structure Rule
explanations.text: Gates BUY alerts only — doesn't affect the batch report score or sell alerts. The current bar must close higher AND make a higher low vs the prior bar, proving the bounce has started. Blocks dead-cat bounces. Backtested: structure-confirmed buys averaged +4.7% over 20 days vs +2.0% unfiltered.

explanations.name: Volume Rule
explanations.text: Gates SELL alerts only. The current bar's volume must be at or above its 20-day average — overbought plus heavy volume means real distribution. Backtested: volume-confirmed sells averaged -2.7% over 20 days vs -1.6% unfiltered. Each rule only gates its own side because backtesting showed it hurt the other.

explanations.name: Action Alert
explanations.text: The ONLY automatic push alert (`app.scheduler.run_action_alert_check`, job id `action_alert_check`, checked every `priority_interval_minutes` — configurable via /priority, default 30) — replaced the earlier separate technical-only Priority Alert and valuation-only Cheap Alert after they proved spammy on their own. Fires ONLY when a watchlist ticker clears EVERY one of 5 bars at once, so it's rare by design, meant to read as 'this is a definite buy right now', not a running reminder: (1) valuation score (see 'Valuation Score') reads 'cheap' or 'very cheap'; (2) technically oversold — mean-reversion trigger score >= `scheduler.priority_min_signals` (default 2 of 3) on the BUY side specifically, never sell; (3) AND that side's confirmation gate passes (bounce structure — a higher close and higher low vs the prior bar — same gate /signals already uses, so this is never a falling knife); (4) positive growth trajectory — both revenue and earnings growth above `scheduler.action_alert_min_growth` (default 0.0, i.e. simply positive); (5) analyst consensus in `scheduler.action_alert_analyst_labels` (default `["buy", "strong_buy"]`). Only once ALL FIVE deterministic-ish bars above pass does it spend a live AI call (`app.llm.build_prompt`, detailed mode) asking the model for its own independent verdict — if the AI's reply doesn't start with 'BUY', the alert is VETOED and nothing sends, even though every other bar passed. This keeps the (slower, costlier) AI check as a final confirmation gate rather than the primary filter, so cost stays bounded to the rare tickers that already cleared everything else. If OPENROUTER_API_KEY isn't set, the AI leg is skipped (treated as passed) rather than blocking the alert, since the other 4 legs are already strict; if the AI call itself fails or returns empty (network hiccup), the ticker is left UNRESOLVED and retried on the next 30-min check rather than either silently vetoing or falsely confirming a real high-conviction setup. Edge-triggered like the alerts it replaced: once a ticker clears everything (and isn't AI-vetoed) it won't re-alert on subsequent checks for the same qualifying streak — it must first drop out of qualifying (any one of the 5 bars fails) and later requalify before firing again. Labeled 'ACTION ALERT:' in the message, includes the AI's own reasoning underneath the usual technical/valuation/target block. State (`_action_resolved`) is in-memory only and resets on every redeploy/restart, same tradeoff as the rest of the app's in-memory alert dedup — after a restart, a currently-qualifying ticker is treated as freshly qualifying and gets a fresh AI check.

explanations.name: Morning Report
explanations.text: Every trading day, 30 minutes after the open (10:00am ET): detailed signals, a fuller AI fundamental summary, a Relative Strength ranking, a Cheap Right Now list (only when at least one favourite reads cheap), and a news digest — for your favourites only. This is the one fully automatic report and cannot be triggered manually; use /signalsplus, /cheap fav, or /news any time for the equivalent content on demand (Relative Strength is currently morning-report-only).

explanations.name: Cheap List / Valuation Ranking
explanations.text: /cheap (watchlist), /cheap fav (favourites), or /cheap TICKER... — ranks EVERY ticker in scope from cheapest to most expensive using the 0-100 valuation score (see 'Valuation Score' below), not just a cheap/not-cheap filter. Shows a compact table (score, ticker, band) sorted ascending, then EVERY computable valuation number per ticker — not just whichever single signal was most extreme — trailing P/E vs its own historical range (plus forward P/E vs that same range when notably cheaper/richer), PEG vs the 1.0/2.0 cheap/expensive lines, and P/S vs its own historical range, e.g. 'Trailing P/E 19.7 is below its entire 4yr range (27.1-786.3), and the forward P/E of 10.5 is cheaper still. PEG 0.57 — paying only 0.57x the earnings growth rate, under the 1.0 undervalued line. P/S 20.3 is below its 4yr average...'. Tickers with zero computable signals (e.g. ETFs like IBIT with no income statement) are listed separately as 'insufficient financial history', never silently dropped — if you ever see fewer rows than tickers in scope, check that footer before assuming something broke. This ranking/number block itself is deterministic (no AI) — the same data always produces the same numbers. When run interactively (not the automatic Morning Report) and OPENROUTER_API_KEY is set, one AI message is appended after the ranking: for a SINGLE scored ticker, a 4-6 sentence 'Why It's Priced This Way' paragraph reasoning over the valuation numbers, growth/margin, the analyst price target's upside/downside, and the overall technical rating together — explicitly told not to invent a different cheap/fair/expensive label than the one already computed, and to flag anything that cuts against that verdict rather than giving a one-sided pitch; for MULTIPLE scored tickers, a 5-7 sentence 'Portfolio Take' synthesis (not a per-ticker recap) naming which names are genuinely cheap with a supportive picture, which look cheap on paper but carry a warning sign, and the single most attractive vs. most-worth-avoiding name. The Morning Report auto-appends a filtered, AI-free version (only the 'very cheap'/'cheap' bands, titled 'Cheap Right Now') so daily noise and AI cost stay low; run /cheap directly any time for the full ranking plus the AI take.

explanations.name: Relative Strength
explanations.text: Shown in the Morning Report: your favourites ranked by (ticker's % return) minus (SPY's % return) over `relative_strength.window_days` (default 20 trading days), strongest first. When several favourites are oversold at once, capital is limited — this tells you which dip has been holding up best relative to the market, i.e. which one to prioritize buying first. Purely computed from price history, no AI involved, so it's fast and free. Skips any ticker whose return can't be computed (insufficient history or a fetch failure) rather than erroring out.

explanations.name: Cheap LEAPS Alert
explanations.text: A daily push scan (10:30am ET, weekdays) of your favourites' LEAPS chains — same scan as /options leaps, but automatic: you only get a message when at least one candidate in that ticker's sample has IV/HV below `options.leaps_alert.iv_hv_threshold` (default 0.9, i.e. the 'cheap' or 'very cheap' bands), instead of having to remember to run /options leaps yourself. One alert per ticker per day (re-arms daily if it stays cheap). Only checks the sample shown in the message, not literally every strike on the full chain — same sample the on-demand scan already shows and reasons over, so this is consistent with what you'd see if you ran /options leaps manually, but it means a cheap strike that fell outside the evenly-spread sample could in theory be missed. Includes the same AI analysis as /options leaps when OPENROUTER_API_KEY is set; skipped (data-only alert) if it isn't.

explanations.name: Position Sizing
explanations.text: Appended to /portfolioanalysis, below the AI's Actions/Add/Risk write-up: a deterministic (non-AI) suggested share count for each watchlist ticker currently oversold (trigger score >= +1), sized to risk `portfolio.risk_per_trade_pct` (default 1%) of `portfolio.account_size` (default $10,000) per trade, with the stop set `portfolio.stop_vol_multiple` (default 2x) daily-volatility moves below entry. Uses the stock's own realized volatility as the volatility input, not a true ATR(14) — a reasonable stand-in, not a precision risk tool, same honesty standard as the IV/HV proxy elsewhere in the app. Computed in Python, not asked of the LLM, because arithmetic should be exact and reproducible. Edit `portfolio.account_size`/`risk_per_trade_pct` in config to match your actual account.

explanations.name: News
explanations.text: /news searches for material news on your favourites and their sectors — earnings surprises, M&A, regulatory action, major guidance or executive changes, macro events hitting the sector. Routine analyst-target tweaks and generic recaps are filtered out; if nothing material happened, that ticker is simply omitted.

explanations.name: Deep Dive
explanations.text: /deepdive [TICKER...] (no ticker → favourites) is /signalsplus with a structured, data-dense AI research report in place of the short summary. The AI receives everything the app has already computed — indicators with exact levels, trend, confirmation gates, day change, P/E, valuation-vs-history with the actual ranges, growth/margin/analyst-consensus numbers, and a near-term options snapshot — and is told to cite those numbers rather than re-derive them, spending its live web search only on what the app can't compute (news, competitors, macro). Five sections per ticker, 1-3 sentences each with every claim anchored to a number or named fact: Technical Setup, Fundamentals & Valuation, Options & Sentiment, News/Catalysts & Competition (with the same no-lazy-earnings-catalyst rule as /signalsplus), and Risks & Macro. Then a 'Trade Plan:' line giving a concrete entry zone (a specific price or range derived from the Bollinger/EMA/valuation levels — deliberately no target or stop), and one bolded BUY/SELL/HOLD closing verdict reflecting a multi-week swing decision. Slower than every other command since it runs a technical scan plus an options snapshot plus one long LLM call per ticker. Same run-to-run variation caveats as everything else using the live-search model.

explanations.name: P/E
explanations.text: Trailing / forward price-to-earnings, shown as context in every report (not scored). 'n/a' means Yahoo doesn't publish a PE for that instrument (e.g. ETFs like IBIT). 'n/m' (not meaningful) means the trailing or forward EPS is zero or negative — the ratio would be a meaningless negative or undefined number, most common on early-stage/unprofitable names.

explanations.name: Analyst Target
explanations.text: Shown as a deterministic 'Target' row alongside the technical/valuation data in every signals/signalsplus/deepdive block, and as an 'Analyst target' line under each ticker's valuation numbers in /cheap — the analyst mean price target and its upside/downside versus the current price (`app.fundamentals.format_target`), plus analyst count and consensus recommendation when available. 'n/a' when Yahoo has no analyst coverage for that instrument (e.g. ETFs). This number is deliberately computed once and shown as plain data rather than left for the AI to restate in its own words — the AI summaries for /signalsplus, /cheap, and /deepdive are still told to weigh this figure (and the overall technical rating) when forming their verdict, but are explicitly instructed never to quote the target's dollar figure or percentage back in their prose, since that would just be a redundant, possibly-slightly-reworded repeat of the number already shown above it.

explanations.name: PE Quality
explanations.text: Shown as a 'PE Quality' row (only when it matters — empty/hidden otherwise) right under P/E in every signals/signalsplus/deepdive block: a flag for when a stock's reported trailing P/E doesn't reflect its recurring earnings power because GAAP net income over the last 4 reported quarters was meaningfully boosted or hurt by a one-off, non-operating item — the textbook example is a large investment mark-to-market gain (ASU 2016-01 requires unrealized gains/losses on equity stakes to hit the income statement, e.g. GOOGL's stakes in SpaceX/Anthropic/etc.), but a big legal settlement, asset write-off, or divestiture gain/loss shows up the same way. Computed from yfinance's quarterly income statement (`app.valuation._pe_quality`): sums the last 4 quarters' 'Net Income' (GAAP) and 'Normalized Income' (Yahoo's own ex-unusual-items figure) and divides each by the latest quarter's diluted share count to get a GAAP-TTM P/E and a core (normalized) P/E — both computed the SAME self-consistent way, deliberately NOT mixed with yfinance's separately-sourced headline trailingPE/trailingEps, which uses its own black-box TTM window and can disagree by a wide margin (confirmed live: GOOGL's headline trailingEps of 19.94 didn't match a plain sum of its last 4 quarters' Diluted EPS of ~13.1). Flags 'inflated' when GAAP income was boosted by a gain beyond `valuation.pe_quality_distortion_threshold` (default 15%) of TTM net income — the reported P/E looks CHEAPER than recurring earnings power supports (confirmed live: GOOGL read ~26% inflated, core P/E ~33 vs GAAP-TTM P/E ~24); 'suppressed' when a charge pushed GAAP income down — the reported P/E looks RICHER than it should (confirmed live: PFE read ~106% suppressed by a litigation-style charge, core P/E ~9 vs GAAP-TTM P/E ~19). Silently omitted (shows nothing) when distortion is under threshold or yfinance doesn't have enough quarterly 'Normalized Income' data to judge (e.g. ETFs, some smaller/foreign filers) — never a false 'normal' claim, just no opinion. The AI summaries for /signalsplus and /deepdive are fed this same fact and told to temper conviction accordingly and (for /deepdive) name the type of item if the data indicates which, but are barred from restating the specific core P/E number or percentage since it's already shown in this row.

explanations.name: Valuation
explanations.text: Shown as a 'Valuation' row in every signals/signalsplus/morning-report/priority-alert block, in /deepdive's Fundamentals & Valuation section, and factored into /portfolioanalysis (including a dedicated cheap-stocks list) — context-only reads (never scored into the mean-reversion trigger score, same tier as P/E) of whether a stock is cheap relative to ITSELF, not the market. Three underlying signals: (1) current trailing P/E vs the stock's own trailing P/E at each of its last ~4 fiscal year-ends (price at that date divided by THAT year's own diluted EPS, not today's — using today's EPS against old prices would badly mislead for fast-growth names, e.g. NVDA's EPS grew ~28x in 4 years); the FORWARD P/E is also judged against that same historical band (shown as e.g. 'PE cheap, fwd very cheap') — context only, doesn't vote; (2) PEG ratio (P/E divided by earnings growth) — the standard Peter Lynch heuristic; (3) current price/sales vs its own historical price/sales band, computed the same way as (1) but with revenue — this is what still gives a real read for currently-unprofitable names where P/E is n/m (e.g. RXRX). IMPORTANT data-safety check: if a stock's financial statements are filed in a different currency than its traded price (common for ADRs — confirmed live: BABA files in CNY, NVO in DKK, both trade in USD), the historical P/E and P/S bands are skipped entirely rather than silently dividing mismatched currencies (this produced a nonsense 'historical P/E of 2.6' for BABA before the fix, against its real trailingPE of 18.2) — PEG alone, already currency-safe from Yahoo's own calculation, still scores in that case. Known simplifications, disclosed rather than hidden: revenue-per-share for the P/S band uses TODAY's share count against PAST revenue (no historical share-count feed either); a volatile single fiscal year (e.g. PFE's 2022 COVID-vaccine earnings spike) can skew that year's historical multiple; a ~4-5yr lookback (yfinance's free-tier limit) is a coarse recent range, not a multi-decade chart. This is meaningfully heavier than a plain P/E fetch (pulls `valuation.history_period`, default 6 years, of price history plus annual financials), so it's cached once per ticker per day like P/E — the first report of the day for each ticker takes a bit longer, everything after that is instant.

explanations.name: Valuation Score
explanations.text: The 0-100 number behind the Valuation row and /cheap's ranking (0 = cheapest, 100 = most expensive) — a single composite built from up to 4 independently-normalized signals, each converted onto its own 0-100 scale before being combined, so nothing gets compared on an apples-to-oranges basis: (1) P/E vs its own history (weight 35%) and (2) forward P/E vs the same band (weight 15%) are each converted via a Z-SCORE (how many standard deviations the current multiple sits from the mean of its own ~4 historical fiscal-year P/Es) passed through the normal distribution's CDF — chosen over a simple min-max scale because a single outlier year (like PFE's 2022 spike) would otherwise compress the rest of the scale into a sliver; a z-score instead treats that outlier as widening the acceptable range, and degrades smoothly rather than hard-clipping for a value outside the historical min/max. (3) PEG (weight 25%) uses a LOGISTIC CURVE centered on the standard 1.0 'fair' line (PEG 1.0 -> score 50, PEG 2.0 -> ~90, PEG 0.5 -> ~25) since it's already growth-normalized and needs no historical band. (4) P/S vs its own history (weight 25%) uses the same z-score/CDF method as P/E — deliberately weighted equal to PEG because it's the only signal that survives for currently-unprofitable names, where down-weighting it would quietly make the score worse exactly where it matters most. WEIGHTS ARE A REASONED JUDGMENT, NOT BACKTESTED: P/E-vs-history gets the most weight as the most time-tested, realized (not estimated) signal; forward P/E gets the least since it leans on analyst estimates. THE KEY BIAS-AVOIDANCE RULE: when a signal is unavailable (no PEG for an unprofitable company, no historical band for an ADR with a currency mismatch, etc.), its weight is redistributed proportionally among whatever remains — never defaulted to a neutral 50, which would silently drag the score toward 'average' for exactly the names with the least data. A ticker with zero computable signals (ETFs) gets no score at all, shown separately, not a fabricated one. All weights and curve parameters are configurable under `valuation.score_weights`/`peg_score_midpoint`/`peg_score_steepness`. Score bands: 0-20 very cheap, 20-40 cheap, 40-60 fair, 60-80 expensive, 80-100 very expensive.

explanations.name: Options Data & Market Hours
explanations.text: /options (leaps and wheel), /deepdive's options section, and the daily Cheap LEAPS Alert all depend on yfinance's free live options bid/ask feed. Confirmed live: outside regular US trading hours (9:30am-4pm ET), that feed goes stale — most strikes show bid=$0.00/ask=$0.00 (dropped by the liquidity filter) even when they logged real trading volume, while only a sparse handful of 'recently touched' strikes (usually deep in/out-of-the-money) retain their last live two-sided quote. A scan run at 5:45am ET on GOOGL — one of the most liquid underlyings there is — came back with zero near-the-money LEAPS candidates purely because of this, not because none exist. When /options or /deepdive comes back empty or short on options data, check the timestamp: if it's outside 9:30am-4pm ET, the app now says so directly ('US markets are closed right now...') instead of leaving you to guess whether the result is real. Re-running during regular hours is the fix, not a config change. The Cheap LEAPS Alert isn't affected in practice since it's scheduled at 10:30am ET by default, already inside the session.

explanations.name: LEAPS Scanner
explanations.text: /options leaps analyzes EVERY qualifying call strike at EVERY expiration in the 1-2yr window (up to `max_expirations`, default 12). Two independent filters must BOTH pass: delta 0.35-0.70 (liquidity-filtered), AND a hard moneyness cap — strike within `max_pct_below_spot` (default 20%) below spot to `max_pct_above_spot` (default 30%) above spot. The cap exists because delta alone is not a reliable 'near the money' proxy for high-volatility names on long-dated options — e.g. a stock with 70%+ realized volatility can show a strike 100%+ above spot still sitting at a moderate delta like 0.40, since Black-Scholes correctly prices in a real (if small) chance of that much movement over ~2 years. That's mathematically fine but not a reasonable swing trade for a retail LEAPS buyer — a strike that far out is a lottery ticket, and a company can always get acquired, disappoint on guidance, etc. The message shows a readable SAMPLE of about `sample_size` (default 20) strikes, spread evenly across both time (expirations) and moneyness (strikes within each expiration) — grouped by expiration, one narrow row per strike, in whole months (e.g. '17mo'). Each row shows the exact IV/HV ratio next to its band label (e.g. '1.18 fair'), not just the label, plus BE (breakeven price = strike + premium paid — what the stock must reach by expiration just to break even). IV/HV bands: 'very cheap' (below 0.7), 'cheap' (0.7-0.9), 'fair' (0.9-1.3, a typical premium), 'rich' (1.3-1.6), 'very rich' (above 1.6, paying well above the stock's own recent volatility). Scanning every expiration this way is what makes 'longer expirations are sometimes too expensive' directly visible — you can watch the premium grow from the nearest to the farthest expiration for the same strike. At the bottom, the AI writes a genuine multi-sentence analysis weighing up to 3 of the best strikes to trade from the full sample shown — NOT simply whichever is cheapest by IV/HV, but weighed together with the technical/fundamental backdrop, whether a farther expiration's extra premium is worth the extra time bought, earnings timing, and how large a move the strike actually needs to pay off (a strike well above spot needs a much bigger move). It closes with exactly one verdict line: 'TRADE — summary', 'HOLD — summary', or 'NO TRADE — summary', bolded in the message. IMPORTANT: IV/HV is a realized-volatility proxy, not a true IV percentile/rank against a year of historical IV — yfinance has no historical IV feed. Calls only. If you run the scan twice and get different results, the two real causes are: (1) the market itself moved between calls — bid/ask/IV shift live during trading hours, changing the numbers; or (2) the AI is a live-search model, so its retrieved context (and therefore its wording/verdict) can differ between calls even at temperature 0, since search results aren't a fixed corpus.

explanations.name: Wheel Scanner
explanations.text: /options wheel scans cash-secured put strikes 1-3 weeks out, averaging ~2 weeks (delta 0.15-0.30, liquidity-filtered) and ranks by annualized yield (premium / capital required, annualized) — here HIGH IV/HV is what you want, since you're selling (the opposite of LEAPS). Candidates whose expiration falls on or after the next earnings date are flagged (not excluded) with a warning, since holding a short put through an earnings surprise carries real gap risk despite the richer premium. Shows the cash-secured-put entry leg only — the covered-call follow-through after assignment isn't scanned, since the app doesn't track your share ownership or cost basis. The AI verdict — TRADE (naming one specific strike from the candidates shown), HOLD, or NO TRADE — is restricted to those candidates only, not a free pick, so candidate selection is deterministic given the same market snapshot; the market itself moving between calls, or the AI's live web search returning different context, are the two real sources of run-to-run variation.

explanations.name: Options Profit Calculator
explanations.text: /opc TICKER STRIKE C|P EXPIRATION [PREMIUM] (`app/commands/opc.py`, `app.options.profit_calc.compute_opc`, `llm.build_opc_prompt`) — analyzes a specific option contract: is its premium cheap, fair, or rich right now, and what's the likely profit/loss outcome by expiration given real news and events, e.g. `/opc NVDA 200 CALL 2026-09-18`. Requires `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` (blocking, like /deepdive) since the AI analysis is the whole point of the command — an earlier version showed a big deterministic price/date P/L grid instead and no AI, which read as noninformative noise rather than an actual answer to 'is this a good trade'; that grid math still runs internally (Black-Scholes, same erf-based normal-CDF as the LEAPS/wheel scanners) but only feeds the AI prompt now, not the displayed message. Fetches the REAL chain: nearest listed expiration/strike to what you typed (exact match not required), that contract's live mid price and IV, plus 90-day realized volatility (`options.opc.hv_window_days`, default 90) to compute an IV/HV cheap/fair/rich read exactly like the LEAPS scanner's — the optional PREMIUM argument overrides the live mid with your own cost basis if you already hold the contract at a different price. Shows a slim deterministic header (spot, strike, premium, IV/HV read, breakeven, max loss = premium × 100 × contracts), then one AI-written analysis (`llm.opc_max_tokens`, default 400) that: (1) judges whether the premium is cheap/fair/rich weighing the IV/HV read (without restating the exact ratio number, which is already shown above it); (2) weighs what that IV implies for the P/L scenarios computed via Black-Scholes at expiration (fed to the prompt as concrete anchor numbers, not re-derived by the model); (3) searches for real, current news/catalysts (earnings date, sector trends, macro) specific to this ticker and explains how they could move price before this expiration; (4) gives a probability-weighted (not guaranteed) likely outcome; (5) closes with exactly one bolded `TRADE`/`HOLD`/`NO TRADE` verdict (same last-matching-line extraction, `app.commands.options._highlight_closing_verdict`, as the LEAPS/wheel scanners). Known simplification, inherited from the underlying Black-Scholes P/L math the AI reasons over: IV is held constant at today's fetched value — a real IV move (e.g. a post-earnings crush) isn't modeled, which is exactly why the AI is told to reason about news/catalysts on top of the raw IV read rather than take the number at face value.
